title: All is opinion
hookLine: everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power (Meditations 12.22)

lines: THE STORY CHANGED, NOT THE WORLD.
cards: A text arrives: "we need to talk." Nothing else. In the next four minutes, the mind can get you fired, dumped, and blamed for something you can't remember doing.
Then the follow-up lands: "about the weekend plans." The words didn't change. The world didn't change.
What changed was the story built around four words. For Marcus, that gap, between what happens and what we make of it, is where much of our trouble lives, and it's the one place we can reach.

teach.b: Way back in book two, Marcus wrote himself a short line. In George Long's translation: "Remember that all is opinion."

In book twelve he comes back to it, more or less: take your opinion away whenever you choose, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you'll find calm water, everything still, a bay without waves.
First, what opinion means here. The Greek word is hypolēpsis: an assumption, the judgment you add to a thing. Not the event, but the label.
"This is a disaster." "She did that on purpose." Second, what Marcus doesn't mean.
He isn't saying nothing is real, or that facts are just viewpoints. The text came. The weekend plans exist.
What's opinion is the weight: harmful, insulting, ruined.

teach.h: THE OPINION IS YOURS TO CHANGE.
ROUND THE HEADLAND, FIND THE BAY.
teach.b: Events aren't in your power. Your reading of them is, at least a little, at least after a breath. That's the hopeful half.
If the storm were out there, you'd have to wait for the weather.
If much of it is in here, you can row toward the bay. Fourth, a neighbor. Marcus links the idea in book two to a Cynic named Monimus, who apparently said that everything is smoke, or vanity.
Marcus takes the sharper edge off it: not that nothing matters, but that what we add to things can be taken away.

how: Readers of Marcus often practice separating what happened from the judgment they've added to it, describing the event plainly and then choosing how to read it.

o: the stillness Marcus says comes when you drop your opinion
a mind so calm it never feels anything at all
a still harbor where Roman sailors waited out storms

games.q: all is opinion. tap the pairs.
p: the judgment we add to a thing
round the headland, find calm water
a Cynic Marcus links the idea to

s: Marcus means that nothing is real and facts are only viewpoints
the event is real; what's opinion is the weight we add to it.
Marcus first wrote "all is opinion" in book two and came back to it in book twelve
2.15 says it in one short line; 12.22 adds the sailor finding calm water.
for Marcus, the hopeful part is that the opinion is ours
events aren't in our power, but our reading of them can change.

games.q: a text says "we need to talk," and nothing else. by Marcus's teaching, where is the trouble right now?
o: in the story you've built around it.
in the person who sent it.
games.why: the words are just words. the weight comes from the opinion we add, and Marcus says that part can be taken away.

practice: Bring up one thing that's bothering you, and say plainly what actually happened, as if you were a camera: who said what, what arrived.
Then notice the label you've stuck on it, unfair, a disaster, typical, and try a different label that's just as honest: inconvenient, unclear, not finished yet.

wordCard.voice: Calm water. Marcus says taking your opinion away is like a sailor rounding the headland into calm water, a bay without waves. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an assumption, a judgment or opinion. Marcus's word in "all is opinion."

carryVoice: Your line: in my power. The event is the event; the label is yours. That's day six hundred thirty-three.
